props.text:
Role: Orient the audience to the conversation.

Talk track: Today we'll move through four topics:

First, what market pressure is making AI harder to scale? 
Second, where is the opportunity for companies that get this right? 
Third, why is IBM positioned to help? 
And fourth, what is the next move for your organization? 

This isn't a product tour. It's a conversation about how AI changes the way the enterprise needs to sense, decide, act, operate, and govern — and highlights the new approaches that will help get you there.

Discovery question: Where would you like to spend the most time today: the market pressure, the operating model, IBM’s role, or possible next moves?

Seller emphasis: Set expectations that IBM will get to solutions, but only after the client problem is clear.

props.text:
Role: Transition into Action.

Talk track: Once the enterprise has contextual understanding, the next challenge is getting that understanding into the flow of work. 

That's Action. 

This is where AI moves from insight to execution across tasks, decisions, workflows, approvals, applications, service, remediation, and business processes.

<Click>

96% of enterprises are already using AI agents in some capacity. 

And with that, the question is whether those agents can operate inside the business. Do they have the right context, access to the right systems, coordination with people and workflows, clear governance, and the ability to adapt when conditions change?

Discovery question: Where do you already have AI-generated insight or agent activity that still does not move cleanly into real work?

Seller emphasis: The buyer anxiety is: “Can AI actually change work, or is it just producing more output?” Keep the distinction sharp. Action is broader than agents. Agents are one mechanism; the goal is coordinated, governed execution.
________________
Statistic
OutSystems, 2026 State of AI Development, April 2026 (n=1,900 IT leaders globally)

props.text: The ROI% and the efficiency% are different metrics — this is the narrative bridge connecting $1.46M Year 1 savings to hours of manual work released, mapping explicitly toward Woolworths' 50% target.
~98% of Planning Analytics work is currently manual (workshop-confirmed). 750 users × ~40 hrs/week × 48 weeks = ~1,440,000 total annual labour hours in scope.
~1,411,200 hours/year of manual work — the efficiency% denominator
Calculate Hours Released by AI in Year 1
Planning Analytics Agent: 375 active users × 4 hrs/week × 48 weeks =
. IBM Bob: ~8,140 developer-hours of realised value (~$814K ÷ $100/hr).
Total gross hours released Year 1: ~80,140 hours
80,140 ÷ 1,411,200 — using 50% adoption, 15% realisation, and 25–30% conservative scaling.
Year 1: ~5.7% of total manual effort automated
Year 1 ramp → Year 2 adoption deepens → Year 3 full adoption + compounding modernisation flywheel. Note: 50% target applies to Planning Analytics; IBM Bob developer gains are additive upside.
$5.2M cumulative net return = the financial expression of this efficiency journey
measures return on investment — a 537% ROI means every $1 invested returns $5.37.
measures how much total manual workload AI has absorbed. These metrics move in the same direction but are calculated differently.
50% North Star — achievable within conservative envelope
of manual planning, coding, and analysis work that Woolworths staff no longer need to perform manually — and that is how dollars become efficiency percentages.
IBM Data & AI | Confidential | Prepared for Woolworths Finance & Planning Team

props.text: This demo showcases an AI-assisted workflow for designing and deploying a Planning Analytics model from scratch. Using Bob with Planning Analytics as the demo interface, the copilot generates TM1 artifacts, creates documentation, and deploys the model through MCP Tools.
